sentences: A colossal wave curls like a claw, about to crash over three boats.
This colour woodblock print by Katsushika Hokusai is often counted among the best-known images in all of Japanese art.
The small box at the upper left gives the series title and the name of this view, with Hokusai's signature written just beside it.
This is the first print in the series Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji.
Around the age of seventy, in 1831, Hokusai issued a print series showing Fuji from many different places, and this scene is one of them.
His publisher, Nishimuraya Yohachi, made a point of advertising the striking new blue used in these prints.
Look at the crest of the wave.
Its white foam splits into claw-like fingers that reach down as if to seize the boats below.
The wave is estimated to stand some ten to twelve metres high, which shows just how small the boats really are.
Hokusai used imported synthetic Prussian blue boldly to achieve the deep colour of the sea.
This fade-resistant blue sparked what is often called a blue revolution in Japanese prints of the 1830s.
Here dark and pale blues overlap to give the wave its depth.
Beneath it, in the boat on the left, the rowers bend low inside the hull.
These were fast cargo boats that carried live fish to the markets of Edo, today's Tokyo, and each one was rowed by eight men.
Now look for tiny Mount Fuji in the distance, nestled between the waves.
The real subject of the picture is not the wave but this snow-capped mountain, and the great curve of the wave frames it.
In the lower boat, too, the rowers crouch and surrender to the swell.
Fragile human beings, the force of nature and the eternal peak are all set against one another in a single, tightly balanced frame.
Some suggest the print is best viewed from right to left, the way Japanese is read.
Notice that the bow of the upper boat on the right also points to the left, straight toward the wave.
As a print, it was produced in thousands of impressions.
When it reached Europe it had a deep influence on artists such as Monet and Van Gogh.
The composer Debussy even put it on the cover of his score La Mer.
Today impressions are held by the Met, the British Museum and many other collections around the world.
Step back and feel how the smallest thing here, the distant Mount Fuji, quietly holds the whole picture together.
